title: Leftmost Column with at Least a One
statement:
This is an interactive problem. A hidden matrix holds only 0s and 1s, and every row is sorted in non-decreasing order (its 0s come before its 1s). Return the smallest column index (0-based) that contains a 1 in any row, or `-1` when the matrix has no 1 at all.

You cannot read the matrix directly. Your function `leftMostColumnWithOne(binaryMatrix)` receives an object with two methods:

- `binaryMatrix.get(row, col)` returns the value at that 0-based position;
- `binaryMatrix.dimensions()` returns `[rows, cols]`.

A solution that calls `get` more than 1000 times is judged wrong.

Each case is written as `[mat]`, the whole matrix. The judge builds `binaryMatrix` from `mat`; your function never sees `mat` itself.
constraints: each row mat[i] is sorted in non-decreasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Reading every cell would take up to 10,000 calls, far over the limit of 1000. Because each row is sorted, its 1s form one block at the right end, so the first 1 in a row can be found by binary search in about 7 calls. Better still, once some row has its first 1 at column `answer`, later rows only matter if they have a 1 to the left of it, so each search can be limited to columns `0` to `answer - 1`. (Walking a staircase from the top-right corner is another way, using at most `rows + cols` calls.)

## Approach

1. Read `rows` and `cols` from `dimensions()`. Set `answer = cols`, meaning "no 1 found yet".
2. For each `row`, binary search the half-open range `[left, right) = [0, answer)` for the first 1.
3. At `mid`, a 1 means the first 1 is at `mid` or earlier, so `right = mid`; a 0 means it is after `mid`, so `left = mid + 1`.
4. When the search ends, `left` is the row's first 1 inside the range, or `answer` itself if the range has none, so `answer = left` keeps the minimum.
5. Return `-1` if `answer` is still `cols`, otherwise `answer`.

## Example 1, step by step

`mat = [[0,0],[1,1]]`, so `rows = 2`, `cols = 2` and `answer = 2`. Row 0: `mid = 1` reads 0, so `left = 2` and `answer` stays 2. Row 1: `mid = 1` reads 1, so `right = 1`; then `mid = 0` reads 1, so `right = 0`. Now `answer = 0`, and the function returns `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(rows · log cols) calls to `get`, at most 100 · 7 = 700.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Scanning each row from the left can cost `rows · cols` calls and breaks the 1000-call limit.
- Use the range `[0, answer)`, not `[0, cols)`: a row with no earlier 1 must leave `answer` unchanged.
- Return `-1`, not `cols`, when there is no 1.
- Rows and columns come from `dimensions()`; the matrix itself is not available.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | the matrix size from `dimensions()` |
| `answer` | leftmost column with a 1 found so far (`cols` if none) |
| `row` | the row being searched |
| `left`, `right` | the half-open search range `[left, right)` |
| `mid` | the column being probed |

narration.2: Ask the matrix for its size; its cells are only reachable through get.
narration.3: cols is a stand-in for 'no 1 found yet', past every real column.
narration.4: Search every row for a 1 to the left of the best column so far.
narration.6: Only columns before answer can improve it, so the range ends there.
narration.7: Keep halving while the range is not empty.
narration.8: Probe the middle column of the range.
narration.9: A 1 here means the row's first 1 is at mid or further left.
narration.10: Keep mid in the range and drop everything to its right.
narration.12: A 0 means every column up to mid is 0 in this row.
narration.15: left is this row's first 1 in the range, or answer itself if there was none.
narration.17: No 1 anywhere gives -1; otherwise return the leftmost column found.
